blocks: Why it fits: the Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/03 Types/12 Modal oscillator models a struck resonating body, and this patch is tuned as tubular bells with a medium decay. The opening of Mike Oldfield's "Tubular Bells" became the theme of The Exorcist. Twelve strokes on one bell is also the midnight chime.

These need the gooseneck microphone of the Vocoder Edition, or a TRRS headset microphone in the headphone jack. Set Mic Gain in the Utility menu before the party. The Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/03 Types/22 Vocoder oscillator puts your voice onto the synth's pitch, so you can speak to the room as a monster or a machine. See Microfreak/UG/19 Appendix B Vocoder.

Why it fits: a looping cycling envelope bends the pitch slightly and opens the filter bands, so whatever you say wavers like a wail. Paraphonic mode is on, so you can hold a minor chord and moan into the microphone for a choir of ghosts.

How to use it: hold a minor chord and say "boo" slowly, or sing a long vowel. Good between songs.

Why it fits: key position controls the vocoder's analysis range, so the same spoken word sounds dark on low keys and thin and alien on high ones. Saying "I see you" across the keyboard is an easy bit, and the name matches.

How to use it: speak one phrase while walking a slow line from high keys down to low ones.

Why it fits: a looping cycling envelope and a filtered Sample-and-Hold LFO wobble the pitch and timbre, so your voice sounds like a toy whose batteries are dying. That is a horror-film trope with a friendly side, good for younger guests.

Why it fits: the filter is open with strong resonance, and the name suggests a low, noisy carrier. Played in a low octave this should give the deepest monster voice of the set.

Performance legibility is the degree to which an audience can understand how a musician's visible actions relate to the sounds they hear. Research on musical interfaces also discusses the related idea of instrumental transparency.

A guitarist's plucking gesture can help an audience connect an action to a note. On an electronic instrument, a key press, a knob turn, or a sequencer may affect sound in ways that are less apparent to a listener.
Visibility alone does not guarantee understanding. Familiarity, timing, and repeated connections between action and sound can help an audience learn how a performance works.

Playing notes on a synthesizer can make some decisions visible while a preset or sequencer supplies other aspects of the sound. A repeating phrase can make the effect of a visible filter adjustment easier to hear.
Improvisation and legibility are separate qualities: a prepared performance can be legible, and an improvisation can involve processes that are difficult to see or understand.
Making Mappings: Design Criteria for Live Performance discusses legibility as an audience's ability to perceive the relationship between gesture and sound.
Engaging the Audience considers how an audience can develop an understanding of an unfamiliar instrument during a performance.
Also called the minor blues or hexatonic blues scale. On C, in its standard textbook form: C E♭ F G♭ G B♭. Steps in semitones: 3 2 1 1 3 2. Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor with an added ♭5.
